Mapping ethnic media landscape in America (2025)

Each circle represents an outlet record. Choose raw Facebook followers or followers per 1,000 residents; circle area is proportional to the selected measure.

Putting audience size in context
Followers per 1,000 residents = Facebook followers ÷ city population × 1,000. For example, 5,000 followers in a city of 100,000 equals 50 per 1,000. The unscaled ratio is also included in the CSV and outlet details. This is a city-size comparison, not the share of residents following an outlet; audiences can be national or international, so values can exceed 1,000.

Population sources and interpretation

U.S. denominators use 2020 Census population counts from the U.S. Census Bureau’s TIGERweb Census 2020 service. They describe incorporated places, Census-designated places, and legal towns or townships, not metropolitan areas. Puerto Rico uses municipio populations (county equivalents); Hato Rey and Río Piedras use their parent San Juan municipio. New York boroughs and neighborhoods use the parent New York city population. These geographic choices are documented per record.

Tijuana uses its urban locality population from INEGI’s 2020 Census. Vancouver uses the city’s 2021 Census population from Statistics Canada, a one-year exception. All other matched denominators use 2020. National, multicity, regional, or ambiguous locations are left blank; county, ZIP-code, and metropolitan populations are not silently substituted for cities.

The denominator is the entire city/locality population, not the size of a particular ethnic or language community. City size and boundaries vary greatly; a network headquartered in a small municipality can have an exceptionally high ratio. The ratio compares later follower counts with an earlier Census baseline and is not a contemporaneous population estimate, a local audience estimate, or a measure of journalistic impact. Do not sum these ratios across outlets. Individual geography names, years, sources, and unresolved-match explanations appear in the CSV and outlet details.

Map coverage and data notes

Each circle-size measure uses its own fixed area scale across filters, without logarithms or a minimum radius for the filled circles. Tiny positive circles have a 2.5-pixel visibility outline; that outline is not part of the area encoding. Counts from the November 2026 collection were often rounded by Facebook (for example, 64K became 64,000). The current CSV’s counts are used as supplied; later changes have not been independently reverified. Shared Facebook audiences should not be summed as unique people. Source coordinates with comma separators or misplaced decimal positions are normalized into valid latitude/longitude ranges. Clearly incorrect points for reviewed city/state records are replaced with Census city reference points; these are not office addresses. The Haitian Times uses an approximate Brooklyn locality point. Other supplied coordinates have not been independently geocoded or verified. Multistate outlets appear at the single coordinate supplied. The map boundaries come from U.S. Atlas v3, derived from U.S. Census Bureau geography.

* Counts include each outlet’s primary language and any non-English secondary publishing languages. Each outlet is counted once per language, so totals across languages may exceed the number of outlet records. English is counted only when it is the primary language. “Asian languages” is an additional aggregate: an outlet with one or more of the defined Asian languages is counted once in that row and also in its individual language rows. Zero-count language categories are hidden for the selected community.

Community classification review

Community affiliation describes the audience an outlet serves; publishing language is evidence, not a one-to-one ethnicity rule. The revised database adds Arab American for Chicago in Arabic and The Arab American News, based on their publisher descriptions. The existing Russian category is retained for Our Texas, which describes a Russian-speaking audience. KETO’s Amharic/East African service is assigned to the existing Black category. Radio Cachimbona is assigned to Latino based on its Salvadoran/Central American focus; the unsupported Telugu entry was removed, and Spanish was not assumed.

French, Portuguese, Kinyarwanda, Swahili, and Somali in African-diaspora outlets are compatible with the Black category; they do not automatically create French or Portuguese ethnic groups. The Haitian Times remains in the Black category as an English-language Haitian-diaspora outlet. Secondary French or Creole was not inferred from its audience. BMORENews.com’s supplied French secondary is retained but not independently confirmed. Missing primary languages remain unspecified. The CSV contains per-record review notes and source links; the accompanying media_record_review_log.csv records individual edits.

Key sources: Chicago in Arabic, The Arab American News, Our Texas, Radio Cachimbona, KETO profile, Amjambo Africa, and The Haitian Times.

How to read these counts

Each CSV row counts as one outlet record. Repeated brands, regional editions, and shared Facebook pages remain separate records; this is not a count of unique owners or unique audiences. The CSV uses full state names and consistent city labels. Boroughs and districts are retained separately in LocalityDetail (for example, Brooklyn under New York City and Hato Rey under San Juan). Multiple locations use semicolon separators. LocationType distinguishes cities, counties, regions, and national records; CoverageScope preserves national reach separately from a physical state label. Explicit multistate records count once in each named state, so state totals can exceed the number of records. National, international, and unresolved locations are reported separately. Language spellings are standardized in the CSV: “Ahmaric” becomes “Amharic,” “Francais” becomes “French,” and the non-language value “1987” is removed from the secondary-language field. “Chinese” and “Mandarin” are combined as “Chinese (Mandarin)”; Cantonese remains separate. The aggregate “Asian languages” includes Chinese (Mandarin), Cantonese, Korean, Vietnamese, Tagalog, Japanese, Punjabi, Thai, Indonesian, Khmer, Nepali, Bengali, and Telugu. It describes the East, South, and Southeast Asian languages present in this dataset, not all languages spoken in Asia; Arabic and Russian remain separate categories. Individual languages are retained, and the CSV’s LanguageCategories column records both individual and aggregate memberships.

How we built the dataset

Sources, inclusion criteria, and measurement notes.

The ethnic and Indigenous media landscape in the United States is large and multifaceted. Our landscape assessment brought together existing databases—available publicly or upon request—with consultation and original online research. Sources included:

  • The News Deserts and Ghost Newspaper databases from the Center for Innovation and Sustainability in Local Media at UNC-Chapel Hill.
  • The State of Local News 2025, from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative.
  • The Center for Community Media’s maps and directories at the CUNY Newmark Graduate School of Journalism.
  • The Indigenous Journalists Association’s Indigenous Media Directory and tribal-newspaper resources; directory access may require membership.
  • Wikipedia’s list of Spanish-language newspapers published in the United States.
  • Consultation with APIAVote to reference its Asian media outlet list, provided through consultation rather than a linked public directory.
  • The Directory of California Ethnic Media (Ethnic Media Services, 2020).
  • ProQuest’s Ethnic NewsWatch (consulted in 2024; subscription access), alongside our own online research.

The initial assessment identified outlets across four communities: Asian American and Pacific Islander, Black, Indigenous, and Latino. The revised database also includes Arab American and Russian outlets identified during the community and language review. To construct a focused research sample from this broader database, we included outlets that maintain (a) an active website and (b) an active public Facebook page.

The charts and map above describe the full supplied database. The CSV does not include a validated field confirming current website and Facebook activity.

Why benchmark Facebook presence?

Facebook offers a practical common reference across outlets with different publishing formats. Pew Research Center’s 2025 survey found that 71% of U.S. adults used Facebook, placing it among the country’s most widely used platforms.

For this study, a public page makes it possible to check whether an outlet is publishing and to observe a follower count using the same platform-level measure.

This is a sampling choice, not a measure of journalistic quality or total reach. Followers may be inactive, located outside the outlet’s community, or shared across outlets. The approach can underrepresent newer organizations, smaller Indigenous or language communities, and outlets whose audiences primarily use other platforms.

A note on dates
The title refers to the 2025 landscape assessment. Facebook counts added in the earlier collection were observed on November 18, 2026; the current CSV also contains subsequent edits. These are not historical 2025 audience measurements, and dates for later edits are not recorded.

Built from ethnicmedialist.csv · Snapshot prepared November 19, 2026 · Population measures added November 19, 2026; language, community, and location labels reviewed and standardized.

Chart totals describe this supplied database, not a census of all ethnic media. All records and map boundaries are embedded in this file; no internet connection is required for the visualizations. External source links require internet access.
